clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive dystrophy caused by NR2E3 mutations that disrupt photoreceptor fate, producing an excess of short-wavelength (S/blue) cones at the expense of rods and other cones
Patients report night blindness from early life together with variable central visual disturbance
Characteristic hypersensitivity to blue light on electroretinography: an unusually large S-cone response with markedly reduced or absent rod responses
The electroretinogram shows similar waveforms under scotopic and photopic bright-flash conditions, reflecting a dominant S-cone contribution rather than normal rod and cone separation
Fundus shows nummular pigmentary clumping along the vascular arcades and frequently cystoid macular changes or schisis
Goldmann-Favre syndrome represents a more severe phenotype within the same NR2E3 spectrum, with vitreous degeneration and retinoschisis
Management is supportive with genetic counselling, low-vision aids and consideration of carbonic anhydrase inhibitors for associated cystoid maculopathy
reference.pathophysiology: Enhanced S-cone syndrome arises from mutations in NR2E3, a nuclear receptor transcription factor that normally directs developing photoreceptor precursors toward a rod fate and suppresses the S-cone programme. Loss of this regulation causes an overproduction of short-wavelength cones and a corresponding deficiency of rods and long/medium-wavelength cones. The abnormal photoreceptor mosaic explains the enhanced blue-cone electrophysiological signal, early night blindness, and the associated retinoschisis, cystoid maculopathy and pigmentary retinopathy seen clinically.
additionalDifferentials: Retinitis pigmentosa with cystoid macular oedema
Vitreoretinal degenerations such as Wagner or Stickler syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Full-field electroretinography demonstrating enhanced S-cone responses and reduced rod responses
Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography for cystoid spaces and schisis
Fundus autofluorescence and colour imaging for nummular pigmentation
Molecular genetic testing for NR2E3 mutations
redFlags: Progressive macular schisis or cystoid change threatening central vision
Marked vitreous degeneration raising the risk of retinal detachment in Goldmann-Favre phenotypes
Early lifelong night blindness prompting confirmatory electrophysiology and genetics
Affected siblings requiring screening given recessive inheritance
reference.prognosis: The condition is typically slowly progressive; many patients retain useful central vision for years but can lose acuity from cystoid maculopathy, schisis or, in severe Goldmann-Favre cases, retinal detachment.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the disorder as congenital stationary night blindness or retinitis pigmentosa without the characteristic enhanced S-cone electroretinogram
Treating cystoid macular change as inflammatory oedema
Overlooking retinoschisis and detachment risk in Goldmann-Favre variants
Failing to recognise NR2E3 as the unifying gene across the phenotypic spectrum
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists; management focuses on treating complications and preserving residual vision
Treat the associated cystoid macular oedema with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors as the mainstay
Manage retinoschisis and monitor for retinal detachment, with vitreoretinal surgery for detachment or severe schisis, particularly in Goldmann-Favre cases
Provide low-vision aids, refractive correction and structured visual rehabilitation
Monitor progression with serial optical coherence tomography, electroretinography and visual fields
Confirm the diagnosis with NR2E3 genetic testing and offer genetic counselling given autosomal recessive inheritance
Refer to inherited retinal disease and ophthalmic genetics services and discuss emerging gene-directed therapies
